_comment: Differentiates the First Words lessons, which were one lesson with the language swapped: identical objectives, an identical Latin-cognates angle, identical prompts and three verbatim-shared answers. Each language now teaches what is actually distinctive about it, in its own shape. Applied by scripts/content/differentiate-first-words.py.

concept.explanation: German greetings follow the hour rather than the person: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend. Hallo ignores the clock and is what you will actually hear most. The habit worth starting on day one is that every German noun takes a capital letter wherever it sits in a sentence, so Kaffee and Nation look like names even in the middle of a line.

lesson.objective: Greet someone at any hour, and meet the capital letter that every German noun wears.
lesson.explanation: German greetings follow the hour rather than the person: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend. Hallo ignores the clock and is what you will actually hear most in a doorway or a shop. The habit worth starting on day one is that every German noun takes a capital letter wherever it sits in a sentence, which is why Kaffee and Nation look like names.

exercises.prompt: This is the first word out of your mouth in a Berlin bakery. What does «Hallo» mean?
exercises.explanation: Hallo is hello. It works at any hour, which is why it is the one greeting worth having by heart.

exercises.prompt: You step into a bakery at nine in the morning. Say the word that greets the baker before anything else.
exercises.explanation: One word before anything else. Say it out loud before you check.

exercises.prompt: German gives a capital letter to every noun. Which pair is capitalised for that reason?
exercises.explanation: Kaffee and Nation are nouns, so they keep their capital anywhere in the sentence. Danke, ja, nein and hallo are not nouns and stay lowercase.

exercises.prompt: Complete the word you say as you come through the door: ___
exercises.explanation: Hallo comes before the request, not after it.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. How many times does somebody say no?
exercises.passage:
— Hallo!
— Hallo.
— Kaffee?
— Ja, danke.
— Noch ein Kaffee?
— Nein, danke.
exercises.explanation: The second offer is refused with nein. The first is accepted with ja.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write exactly what you hear, including both words.
exercises.explanation: Two words, both of which you now own.

concept.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.

lesson.objective: Greet someone in Spanish, and meet the opening question mark that Spanish puts in front.
lesson.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.

exercises.prompt: A friend says this to you in Madrid before anything else is said. What does «Hola» mean?
exercises.explanation: Hola is hello. It fits any hour, which is why it is the one greeting worth having by heart.

exercises.prompt: Spanish marks a question at both ends. Which line is written correctly?
exercises.explanation: The upside-down mark opens the question and the ordinary one closes it. Spanish never uses just one.

exercises.prompt: You meet a friend in Madrid. Greet them before anything else is said.
exercises.explanation: One word before anything else. Say it out loud before you check.

exercises.prompt: Complete the greeting you give a friend: ___
exercises.explanation: Hola comes first; the rest of the sentence waits.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange and count the questions in it.
exercises.explanation: Two of the lines open with the upside-down mark. The other four are statements.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write exactly what you hear, including both words.
exercises.explanation: Two words, both of which you now own.

concept.explanation: Portuguese greets by the hour, but one word here behaves differently from every language around it: obrigado is not fixed. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the person speaking rather than the person being thanked. Get that right on day one and you will sound like yourself rather than like a phrasebook.

lesson.objective: Greet someone in Portuguese, and learn why thanks changes shape depending on who is speaking.
lesson.explanation: Portuguese greets by the hour, but one word here behaves differently from every language around it: obrigado is not fixed. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the person speaking rather than the person being thanked. Get that right on day one and you will sound like yourself rather than like a phrasebook.

exercises.prompt: It opens every conversation in Lisbon. What does «Olá» mean?
exercises.explanation: Olá is hello. It fits any hour, which is why it is the one greeting worth having by heart.

exercises.prompt: You meet a neighbour in Lisbon. Greet them before anything else is said.
exercises.explanation: One word before anything else. Say it out loud before you check.

exercises.prompt: A woman is the one speaking, and she is thanking a colleague. Which form is hers?
exercises.explanation: Obrigada agrees with the woman speaking. Obrigado is what a man says, and obrigados is for a group.
This is the masculine speaker form. A woman says obrigada, and both mean the same thing to the person hearing them.

exercises.prompt: Complete the greeting you say as you arrive: ___
exercises.explanation: Olá comes before the request, not after it.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write exactly what you hear. The speaker is a woman.
exercises.explanation: The recording is a woman speaking, so the thanks she gives is obrigada.
